Why Accuracy is Misleading in Clinical AI

In our held-out test cohort of 39 patients, 26 have crowding (66.7%). If a naive dummy model simply predicted "crowding" for every patient without looking at pixels, it would achieve 66.7% accuracy. Our neural network scored only 64.1% (25/39), misclassifying 9 crowding patients (False Negatives: 34.6% miss rate) and 5 healthy patients.

CRITICAL SCIENTIFIC AUDIT: With small N=39, each single error changes test accuracy by ~2.56%. Test AUC ~0.70 confirms this is an experimental pipeline benchmark, not a diagnostic medical device.

          Honest Negative Audit: Saliency Heatmaps Do Not Isolate Problem Teeth Above Random Chance
        

        

          In explainable vision benchmarks, an explanation is validated via the pointing game: 
          if the model genuinely detects rotated front teeth, its attention heat map must sit on the dentist-annotated problem teeth significantly more often than a random region (Lift > 1.0).
          With a median lift of 0.95, the heat maps land on problem teeth *no more than random chance*. 
          The model relies heavily on background lip retractors, gum lines, and saliva reflections. 
          Heat maps must be interpreted as "what arbitrary pixels stimulated the weights", never as clinical proof of malocclusion.

CRITICAL EVALUATION CAVEATS

        
Scientific limitations and ethical AI disclosures

      

      
    

    

      

        

          
1. Weak Model Performance

          

            Test ROC-AUC is 0.701. Overall test accuracy is 64.1%, which is below the majority-class baseline (66.7%). A model that simply guessed "crowding" on every photo achieves higher accuracy.
          

        

        

          
2. Uncalibrated Softmax Probabilities

          

            The model's confidence scores frequently cluster at extremes (>99% or <1%) due to uncalibrated neural net logits over small training data (N=192). These scores are uncalibrated weights, not real patient probabilities.
          

        

        

          
3. Operational Proxy, Not Diagnosis

          

            "Crowding" is operationalized as $\ge 1$ tooth marked by dentists as rotated (TT) or misaligned (TM). It does not represent formal orthodontic diagnosis (e.g., Little's Irregularity Index, Bolton ratio, or arch length discrepancy).
          

        

        

          
4. Negative Pointing Game Result

          

            Median lift is 0.95, meaning the model's heat maps land on problem teeth *less often than random chance*. The model exploits confounding cues (cheek retractors, lighting highlights, gums). Saliency maps show arbitrary attention, not clinical proof.
